title: 5.1 Hedonic model
text:
The primary methods utilised to quantify the premium or capitalisation of energy efficient amenities are either through the discrete choice framework or a hedonic approach following Rosen (1974), Lancaster (1966) and Brown and Rosen (1982). In both these methodologies, it is assumed that the market is competitive with a short-term fixed supply. Moreover, consumers maximise their utility function by weighing a home’s attributes, price and individual trades while staying within budget constraints. Most literature estimating price premiums on energy efficiency labels or energy performance utilises a hedonic model, and this thesis will do the same.
The hedonic model essentially consists of regressions of house value against the characteristics of the unit that determine the value. As a simple example, the dwelling price function can be computed as follows:
\[
V = f(X,G,Q,E)
\tag{6.1}\]
Where V represents the market value of the property (here transaction price); X is a vector of variables describing property characteristics; G is a vector of geographical factors which describes the surroundings of the property and any location attributes (e.g., distance to the central business district, etc.). Q is a vector of variables quantifying the quality/condition of the property, and E represents a vector of energy-efficient variables. To quantify the attribute’s effect on price in an econometrics setting, the majority of studies employ a hedonic regression, as will we. As Figure Figure 2.2 shows, most studies use a logarithmic transformation for their dependent variable, as demonstrated below:
\[
\ln(V) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \mathbf{X} + \beta_{2} \mathbf{G} + \beta_{3} \mathbf{Q} + \beta_{4} \mathbf{E} + e
\tag{6.2}\]
Where e is the error term capturing unobserved factors affecting property prices. Malpezzi (2002) points out that the log-linear form has a couple of advantages. Among the benefits he points out is that taking the logarithm of the dependent variable offers a more straightforward and more appealing interpretation. As an example, if the coefficient of a variable representing energy efficiency, such as the label B, is 0,065, then the approximation of the percentage change can be derived using the method constructed by Halvorsen and Palmquist (1980),
which is \(e^{coefficient}-1\). This means that energy label B will add 6.72% more value to the property. Furthermore, by transforming the dependent variable using natural logarithms, we can reduce the issue of heteroskedasticity. In statistics, heteroskedasticity arises when the error term has varying variance across different levels of the independent variables—for example, considering a regression model where we want to predict housing prices based on dwelling size. Let’s assume that our data shows that the price varies a lot more for smaller properties than for more extensive properties. If we fail to account for this heteroskedasticity, then it will lead to inefficient estimates of our standard errors.
In an ideal setting, we would like to observe house prices of identical properties over time and rewind to manipulate their energy performance to different levels, observing the resulting price changes. However, in our case, such experiments are not feasible in reality. Instead, we rely on statistical methods and data on various factors that constitute the properties attributes, including energy performance, to estimate how changes in these factors affect house prices. We will turn to the Ordinary Least Square (OLS) regression for statistical methods. A standard tool to quantify how changes, such as improving energy efficiency, affect property prices. However, as with any statistical analysis, specific problems may arise and must be addressed before conclusions can be reached without the risk of biased estimations. One problem is that this study relies on a sample that is not randomised. When a sample lacks randomisation, there is a risk of biased estimated effects, which can significantly affect the conclusion drawn from the study. The degree of bias hinges on the correlation between the error term and the independent variable, e.g., the energy performance of the property. If the error term correlates with the variable, it introduces endogeneity, which can skew the results. This correlation can lead to either overestimating or underestimating the variable coefficient.
Moreover, to quantify the causal effect of a variable, for example, energy performance, one must consider other valued attributes of the property. However, given Equation 6.2, energy performance (E) might be linked to the presence or absence of various energy-efficient attributes within the property. These features typically encompass lighting and heating systems, insulation quality, water heating, window glazing and construction years. This suggests that there is a correlation between Q and E. Consequently, even if we were to add a variety of variables into our estimation, we run the risk of introducing potential multicollinearity to our estimates.
Furthermore, another significant challenge in estimating the causal effect is omitted variable bias. Omitted variable bias occurs when important variables are not accounted for in the model. In other words, if we do not account for a variable that influences both the sales price and the property’s energy performance, then we will incorporate that effect into the variable of interest and thereby either overestimate or underestimate the true effect. Take, for instance, energy performance and construction year. These two variables often correlate, in particular since that building standards have changed such that new buildings must be within a specific energy performance range. Construction years can positively affect the sales price of the property and its energy performance. However, when a variable, such as construction year, is omitted from the regression model, then we introduce the risk of overestimating or underestimating the impact of energy performance.
A number of scholars have pointed out that the traditional hedonic model suffers from sample selection bias (see e.g. Stenvall et al. (2022), Wilhelmsson (2019), Næss-Schmidt et al. (2015)). This is a bias that occurs when using non-random data for statistical analysis. As Stenvall et al. (2022) point out in their study, energy-efficient and non-energy-efficient properties might differ in terms of characteristics, i.e. energy-efficient properties might have unique attributes that distinguish them from properties that do not prioritise energy efficiency. Therefore, the causal effect might be distributed non-randomly. In general, one can expect that older buildings tend to have lower energy efficiency than newer buildings. Consequently, as stated by Stenvall et al. (2022), when performing analyses, there arises a potential discrepancy between the two groups, i.e. energy, efficient and non-energy efficient properties, in relation to the age of the property. Even though one does control for age, there remains uncertainty regarding the accuracy of the model’s representation of this relationship. This uncertainty extends to the structure of the relationship, whether it’s linear or non-linear.
It is crucial to acknowledge the challenges faced with when conducting a statistical analysis, as they can pose significant challenges to the interpretation of results. Throughout this thesis, it is imperative to remain mindful of these biases. Next, we shift our focus on to the empirical strategy best suited for addressing various challenges outlined above.

title: 5.2 Estimation Strategy
text:
We will begin by estimating the impact of EPC labels on transaction prices to determine if consumers are willing to pay more for energy-efficient dwellings. To do this, an OLS regression with fixed effects is estimated. This model will lay the foundation as our baseline model and resemble the majority of regressions from the literature, particularly studies by Næss-Schmidt et al. (2015) and Wahlström (2016). For the baseline model, we begin by estimating a parsimonious version of the baseline model, then gradually introduce various control variables, resulting in the final form of our baseline regression equation as follows:
\[
Ln(P_{izt}) = \beta EE_{i} + \mathbf{\gamma X_{i}} + \mathbf{\delta Q_{i}} + \mathbf{\eta G_{i}} + \boldsymbol{\tau_{t}} + \boldsymbol{\mu_{z}} + \boldsymbol{\upsilon_{zt}} + \epsilon_{izt}
\tag{7.1}\]
The dependent variable \((Ln(P_{izt}))\) denotes the natural logarithm of the transaction price of dwelling (i) at four-digit postal code (z) at month (t). The variable of interest is denoted as \((EE_{i})\) and represents the EPC label of dwelling (i). Vector () contains structural characteristics of property, such as living space, number of rooms and floors. The vector \((\mathbf{Q_{i}})\) contains factors quantifying the general condition of the property, such as construction year and year of significant renovation. The structure of the variables from the \((\mathbf{X_{i}})\) and \((\mathbf{G_{i}})\) aligns with the majority of the literature. For example, as pointed out in Chapter 4.1, we follow the approach of Jensen et al. (2016) by structuring the year of construction for properties into periodic bins. Jensen et al. (2016) grouped the years into periods reflecting both building tradition and energy performance. The only difference between our variable and theirs is an additional bin for the newer years, as our sample spans a longer period. By structuring the variable, as well as other continuous variables, in a categorical format, we are able to capture non-linear effects. Furthermore, ( ) represents the neighbourhood structure of properties. The vector comprises several geographical characteristics, including population density at the 1 km grid level. All continuous control variables have been logarithmised. The previous chapter, Chapter 4, presents details on all the variables used in our analysis, including their structural forms.
% fixed effects :
The sample of this analysis spans a long period of time, raising concerns about temporal variation in property prices over the time period. Factors such as seasonality, economic conditions and policy changes all have the potential to impact property prices. To account for this, we include month and year-fixed effects, denoted as \(\boldsymbol{\tau_{t}}\). Moreover, as pointed out earlier in this paper, location plays a vital role as a determinant of property prices. Even though we account for some neighbourhood characteristics, there is still a great risk of unobserved heterogeneity in local market conditions such as school districts, demographic characteristics or other neighbourhood amenities that we do not account for. Therefore, we include 4-digit postal code fixed effects, denoted as \(\boldsymbol{\mu_{z}}\), to control for spatially correlated factors that can influence property prices. With it, we reduce omitted variable bias and improve the robustness of the estimated effects. Furthermore, the housing market can vary significantly, not just by area but also over time within the same area. For example, certain areas might experience seasonal demand fluctuations, infrastructure developments or local economic changes that impact housing prices differently over time. By interacting with the time and postal code fixed effects, we account for localised temporal trends in housing prices. This further mitigates omitted variable bias, which arises from factors that vary both by location and over time. The interaction is denoted as \(\boldsymbol{\upsilon_{zt}}\)
As pointed out in the introduction, the majority of papers do not incorporate additional information in their analysis from the EPC reports related to the renovation potential. In order to deepen our understanding of the impact of energy efficiency on property prices, the baseline model is extended by incorporating additional information derived from the EPC reports, specifically related to energy-efficient renovation potential. Thus, we add the vector \(\mathbf{\phi EER_{i}}\) to Equation 7.1 Equation \(\ref{eq: baseline model}\), resulting in the final regression equation taking the following form:
\[
Ln(P_{izt}) = \beta EE_{i} + \mathbf{EER_{i}} + \mathbf{\gamma X_{i}} + \mathbf{\delta Q_{i}} + \mathbf{\eta G_{i}} + \boldsymbol{\tau_{t}} + \boldsymbol{\mu_{z}} + \boldsymbol{\upsilon_{zt}} + \epsilon_{izt}
\tag{7.2}\]
Here, the vector \(\mathbf{\phi EER_{i}}\) (Energy efficient Renovations) denotes a set of property-specific control variables related to their renovation potential as specified by the following equation:
\[
\mathbf{EER_{i}} = \phi_{1} LabelJump_{i} + \phi_{2} TECS{i} + \phi_{3} TICP_{i} + \mathbf{\phi_{4} RS_{i}}
\tag{7.3}\]
where \(LabelJump_{i}\) is a categorical variable representing the number of EPC labels a property would advance from its current label upon implementing all renovation suggestions made in the EPC report. \(TECS_{i}\) represents the total energy cost saved for the property from implementing all renovation suggestions, while \(TICP_{i}\) represents the total investment cost needed to implement the profitable renovation suggestions. In order to interpret \(TECS_{i}\) and \(TICP_{i}\) as elasticity’s we take the natural logarithm of both variables. However, this leads to a log-0 problem as many observations have zero in both variables. Therefore, we add the constant equal to one before taking the logarithm to overcome this issue.
Finally, the vector \(\mathbf{RS_{i}}\) (Renovation suggestions) contains dummy variables indicating the types of renovations that are required, such as renovating the roof or attic renovation, renovating the building walls or conversion to district heating. \(\mathbf{\phi EER_{i}}\) allows us to capture the static role of the EPC label while also considering the evolving potential for increased energy efficiency and further energy savings. This allows us to determine if home buyers are willing to pay a premium for homes that are already energy efficient as well as those that offer the potential for further enhancements in energy efficiency. As a result, we obtain a more thorough study of the economic gains associated with energy efficiency in the housing market. Additionally, these factors assist in accounting for potential endogeneity and omitted variable bias caused by unobserved renovation characteristics.
Furthermore, As discussed in Capter 3, all related empirical studies on the Danish housing market have focused exclusively on detached houses. On the other hand, as shown in Capter 4.1, our unique dataset encompasses a diverse range of property types. These property types differ both in structural characteristics and market dynamics. As a result, it is critical to recognise that the impact might vary significantly between property types. The model specified in Equation 7.2 was estimated across different property type segments to assess this hypothesis.
Finally, we attempt to quantify the effect from a tighter building regulations that took place on 1. January 2018. The regulation increased the energy performance standards for new buildings and set stricter regulations for renovations on existing properties such that the renovations made meet a minimum energy efficiency standard. Thereby, enforcing that when renovations on existing buildings take place, they truly improve energy efficiency towards buildings. To quantify the policy effect, we split our sample by the date of the policy such that one sub-sample represents the market before the policy took place and the other after the policy took place. Then we run model equivalent to Equation 7.2 on both sub-samples.

title: 6.1 Main results
text:
Model 6
The key results of the analysis are summarised in Table 8.1. Models 1 to 4 estimate Equation 7.1, incorporating additional control variables and fixed effects, until reaching the complete specification of Equation 7.2 in Model 6. The EPC labels are all highly significant at the 0.01% level for all models.
Model 1 has a parsimonious specification. The model includes only EPC labels and basic property characteristics to establish a baseline understanding.
As highlighted in Figure 4.3, there is a noticeable relationship between energy-efficient labels and the year of construction. While newer properties generally exhibit better energy efficiency due to updated building standards, relying solely on construction years may not fully capture all aspects of energy efficiency, given potential changes over a building’s life cycle until its sale. Therefore, additional factors are added in Model 2, such as energy-related attributes, roof and wall material of the property, along with the timing of significant property renovations categorised over periodic intervals.
Moreover, one might argue that the number of rooms is insufficient, as it leaves out important quality details, such as the presence of a garage, conservatory, pool, etc. Therefore, in Model 3, we add additional structural features, such as whether the property has a detached or built-in garage, outhouse or carport, as well as a swimming pool. Finally, fine-grained geographical characteristics of property surroundings are added in Model 4 to further control for micro factors.
Excluding Model 2, the relationship between EPC labels and property prices strengthens as more property characteristics and external features are considered, showing an upward trend. With label D as the reference category, Model 4, the main specification for Equation 7.1, reveals that properties with A2020, A2015, and A2010 labels command average price premiums of 18.6%, 16.4%, and 11.3%, respectively, compared to properties with a D label. Additionally, properties labelled B and C transact at average premiums of 7.6% and 4.7%, respectively. In contrast, properties with less energy-efficient labels E, F, and G are sold at price discounts of 7.9%, 15.8%, and 36.5%, respectively.
From Model 4, we obtain an \(R^2\) of 0.6485, indicating that the model can explain 64.85% of the variance in property prices, reflecting a strong overall fit. However, we obtain a within \(R^2\) of 0.382, which shows that we capture 38.2% of the variation in property prices within the fixed-effects clusters. The low within \(R^2\) suggests significant residual variation within these groups, implying that while the fixed effects account for some local and temporal factors, unobserved influences remain.
The price premiums found in Model 4 for labels A2020, A2015, and A2010, as well as the price discounts for labels F and G, are significantly higher than the label effects reported by Jensen et al. (2016) and Næss-Schmidt et al. (2015). This discrepancy can be attributed to several factors: our study incorporates more comprehensive control variables, treats the three A-labels as individual groups rather than a single group, spans a much longer time period, and includes a significantly larger sample size.
As noted in 3. Literature review, few studies have explored additional features from EPC reports, such as renovation suggestions and energy-efficiency potential. Considering economic rationale, one might assume that home buyers evaluate properties not only by their current energy efficiency but also by their potential for future enhancements as a long-term investment.
Therefore, Models 5 and 6 incorporate additional characteristics taken from the EPC reports, as detailed in 5.2 Estimation Strategy, to assess the potential for improving property energy efficiency through renovations suggested in the reports.
Furthermore, leveraging our unique dataset enables comprehensive coverage across the entire country. However, given the nationwide sample, it is imperative to recognise the potential market dynamics over time within specific areas. Therefore, Model 6 introduces an interaction fixed effect between time and 4-digit postal code fixed effects.

title: 6.1 Main results
text:
EPC labels
With the added renovation characteristics, we see a significant drop in the label effect, particularly for energy-efficient labels. From our final model, Model 6, we find that once renovation potential indicators are accounted for, the price premiums for energy-efficient labels A2020, A2015, and A2010, compared to label D, are measured at 7.7%, 6.4%, and 2.6%, respectively. Additionally, labels B and C are sold on average at 2.2% and 2.0% higher prices than a D-labelled property, respectively, whereas properties with labels E, F, and G are sold for average discounts of 6.2%, 12.5%, and 28.7%, respectively.


Energy sources and systems
Aside from the energy-efficiency labels, we find that consumers are concerned about the energy source and systems. Properties with natural gas, oil, or a mix of electricity and oil are sold at average discounts of 2.6%, 10.6%, and 12.9%, respectively, compared to properties relying solely on district heating as a heat source.
Conversely, properties with only electricity or a mix of electricity and district heating as heat sources are sold at average premiums of 1.9% and 5.4%, respectively, compared to properties relying only on district heating.
Furthermore, we find that properties with solar heating, solar cells, or heat pumps installed are sold, on average, with price premiums of 1.9%, 3.3%, and 0.7%, respectively, compared to properties without these systems. However, the effect from heat pumps is relatively unstable across Models 3 to 6, indicating that the effect may not be robust. In the chapter on robustness testing, we will investigate this further.


Renovation variables
In contrast to the energy sources and systems, we find that consumers pay significant attention not only to the present condition and characteristics of the property but also to the future potential in terms of the property’s energy efficiency.
In Model 6, the effect of the potential energy label that a property can achieve by implementing all renovation suggestions stated in the EPC reports shows a clear non-linear relationship.
In comparison to properties without potential energy labels stated in the reports, we find that the effect of a one-letter increase in the potential energy label, resulting from implementing all stated renovation suggestions, has a fairly marginal price premium of only 0.4%.
However, as the potential energy label gets higher, the higher the positive effect on property prices. As soon as we reach a four-letter increase, the effect starts to diminish and becomes negative once we reach a six-letter increase or greater. This might indicate that while home buyers appreciate energy-efficiency potential, there comes a point where further increases in energy-label rating potential might not justify higher property value. Instead, a significantly higher rating potential may signal a greater need for renovations, leading to a negative impact.
Furthermore, in Models 5 and 6, the impact of the total energy cost saved from implementing all renovation suggestions and the estimated investment cost from implementing profitable renovations are both negative and highly significant. One might have expected the signalling effect of potential energy savings to yield a positive impact. However, the effect of both variables on property prices is considerably modest and inelastic, suggesting that potential home buyers may not prioritise the estimated energy cost savings or the expenses associated with recommended renovations.
On the other hand, with regard to the types of renovations recommended in the reports, we observe that several categories have significant effects on property prices. For instance, properties with proposed upgrades to district heating sell for an average 7.8% higher price than those that do not. District heating relies on existing infrastructure, which then only requires adjusting the heating system, making this option highly valued by home buyers.
Moreover, properties that have renovation suggestions related to windows or doors are sold at an average discount of 5.3% compared with those with no window or door renovation suggestions.
Additionally, while home buyers generally perceive heat pumps to add value to a property, the requirement to install them for higher energy efficiency negatively impacts property prices. This could be due to significant upfront expenses, including equipment and labour costs, which may discourage buyers.
However, it is worth noting that our dummy variable indicating whether a property has installed heat pumps includes all types of heat pumps. In future studies, it may be valuable to distinguish between different types of heat pumps, such as vertical ground-source heat pumps, horizontal ground-source heat pumps, and air-source heat pumps. These types can vary considerably in terms of labour, installation, and equipment costs.
One explanation for why we find that the types of renovations have a significantly higher impact on property prices than the estimated energy-saving cost and investment cost might be that consumers pay more attention to broader renovation characteristics, as the estimated cost benefits and investment expenses are too general.
In addition, both the estimated energy consumption and energy savings may not necessarily reflect home buyers’ energy consumption patterns. Therefore, consumers might pay less attention to the given estimates and more to the broader characteristics. This is consistent with the findings of Christensen et al. (2014), who find that the estimated cost benefits and investment expenses in the reports have limited impact on energy-efficient renovations.

title: 6.1 Main results
text:
Overall findings
Overall, the results from the table show interesting trends regarding energy efficiency and property prices.
In Models 1 to 4, where we successively add control variables related to property features and neighbourhood characteristics, the price premiums and price discounts increase, excluding Model 2. However, once we introduce renovation-potential features of properties in Model 5, we observe a significantly lower price premium for energy-efficient labels and a price discount for non-energy-efficient labels.
The effect diminishes further when we include the interaction fixed effect between time and 4-digit postal code, emphasising the importance of including comprehensive property characteristics in hedonic pricing models, as the previous impact of EPC labels on property prices was most likely confounded by the underlying renovation potential.

title: 6.2 Market Segment: Property Type
text:
Energy Sources and Systems
This chapter will explore the relationship between energy efficiency and property prices across different property types. Unlike prior studies focusing solely on detached houses, our analysis encompasses detached houses, row houses, duplexes, and apartments. We estimate a model specification equivalent to Equation 7.2 for all the subgroups. Model 2 estimates are for detached houses, Model 3 for row houses, Model 4 for duplexes, and Model 5 for apartments. The results are presented in Table 9.1.
The results show that most EPC labels have the expected signs and are significant at the 1% level, with some exceptions in Models 2 and 3, i.e. for duplexes and apartments. For apartments, we find that label C is statistically insignificant. In Model 4, labels A2010, B, C and E are found to be insignificant, whereas labels A2020 and G are significant at the 5% level, and labels A2015 and F are significant at the 10% level. Additionally, the results for the duplex sample show far less significance in all variables accounted for compared to other property types. These inconsistencies in Model 4 may be due to the significantly smaller sample size (8,236 observations), which could affect the reliability of the results. Consequently, this chapter focuses mainly on detached houses, apartments, and row houses.
The impact of EPC labels on property prices varies significantly across property types. Detached houses exhibit the highest price premiums for energy-efficient labels. Compared to label D, home buyers of detached houses are willing to pay a premium of 15.2%, 16.6%, 9.9%, and 8.7% more for labels A2020, A2015, A2010, and B, respectively.
Interestingly, for apartments, the price premiums for energy-efficient labels are much lower. The estimated premiums are equivalent for labels A2020, A2015, and B, measured at 3.7%, whereas for label A2010, the price premium is 5.4%. Row houses show label effects that are relatively consistent compared to the full sample estimates to some degree.
A notable trend is the diminishing returns on energy efficiency labels across the property type segment. The price premium diminishes for detached houses and row houses once the most energy-efficient label is achieved. Similarly, for apartments, the price premium decreases for labels A2015 and A2020, where the premium is nearly equivalent to that of the B label, with only marginal differences. This pattern indicates that as buildings get more energy-efficient, the additional advantages acquired by home buyers tend to diminish. Moving from a D to an A classification delivers significant utility gains; however, upgrades within the A category may result in declining returns. In other words, if a property reaches a specific efficiency level, future renovations may not considerably improve its appeal, or the increased efficiency may not convert into a corresponding rise in perceived value.
The price impact from different heating sources and systems varies across property types. Our results indicate that district heating is the primary heat source, which home buyers prefer when investing in detached houses or apartments. For detached houses, there is only one heating source that trumps district heating: wood pellets, which give a premium of 3.5% compared to district heating. For apartments, the preference for district heating is less pronounced. Apartments with district heating and electricity are sold at a 2% premium, those with only electricity at a 7.1% premium, and those with electricity and wood pellets at a 39.2% premium. The price premium for apartments heated with both electricity and wood pellets seems unusually high, indicating potential missing information in our analysis.
Moreover, detached houses and apartments that are using fossil fuels as the main energy source are found to be sold on average at a lower price compared to those with district heating. Specifically, detached houses and apartments that are solely dependent on natural gas as heating source are sold at a price discount of 7.8% and 3.7%, respectively. Properties with oil as the primary heat source are sold with price discounts of 14.3% for detached houses, 6.6% for duplexes and 5.1% for apartments.
Interestingly, our results indicate that the apartment market is the only property market that acknowledges a value in heat pumps, whereas the effect of the presence of heat pumps in other property types is statistically insignificant. We find that apartments are sold on average at a higher price of 1.1% if they come with a heat pump.
For solar heating and solar cells, we find that the presence of these heating systems is only valued for detached houses and apartments. A detached house is sold on average at a 1.4% higher price if it has solar cells, whereas apartments are sold on average at a 2.4% higher price. If the solar heating system is present in a detached house, we find that the house is sold on average at a 0.6% higher price, and for apartments, the premium is 1.1%. Although we find price premiums for these components, our results indicate that their importance is somewhat lower than that of the heating source in both detached houses and apartments.
crumbs: 9  6.2 Market Segment: Property Type

title: 6.2 Market Segment: Property Type
text:
Renovation Characteristics
Finally, the effect of energy-efficiency potential on property prices differs across property types. In terms of energy label potential from implementing all renovation suggestions, we find only a significant price impact for detached houses and partially for apartments. Similar to our full sample Model, having the ability to go up by one or two EPC labels has a positive effect on prices for detached houses, but once a property reaches the potential to go up by three or more EPC labels, the effect becomes negative, leading to lower property prices.
We only find that a one-letter or three-letter increase has a significant price effect for apartments. Surprisingly, the results indicate that apartments with a one-letter improvement potential have a negative effect on prices, whereas the potential to move up by three labels has a positive effect on apartment prices. One might have expected that the price effect from the potential of a one-letter increase would either be insignificant or marginal. The negative price effect may arise because potential buyers do not perceive a single-letter improvement as enough benefits to justify the potential costs associated with it, whereas a three-letter improvement could signify a more substantial and worthwhile upgrade.
Moreover, we find similar anomalies in terms of total investment cost and total energy cost across property types. Again, the variables are only effective for detached houses and apartments. Interestingly, while increased estimated investment costs for profitable renovations have a negative impact on detached house prices, higher potential total energy savings yield a positive effect. This pattern aligns with economic theory, where perceived increases in energy savings costs are positively correlated, while increased investment costs have a negative impact.
However, unlike the effect found in the full sample, the effect from total energy costs saved for detached houses is significant at the 10% level. Conversely, this trend is flipped for apartments, where higher expected investment expenditures for profitable renovations have a positive impact on unit pricing, while potential total energy cost savings show a negative effect.
This result does strike as a relatively odd one, yet it’s worth noting that the estimated investment cost for profitable renovations and total cost saved from all renovations are at the building level. Unlike detached houses, the estimated energy cost saved and investment cost for profitable renovations for apartments are for the whole apartment block.
Therefore, the cost and benefits are shared across the entire building. This collective arrangement may influence how these benefits are perceived. Overall, regardless of property type—detached house or apartment—the impacts of investment and energy cost benefits are relatively inelastic. However, the implications for property prices resulting from renovation potential in these segments necessitate further investigation.
crumbs: 9  6.2 Market Segment: Property Type

title: 6.2 Market Segment: Property Type
text:
Apartments versus Detached Houses
Overall, we find significant differences between property types, particularly between apartments and detached houses. The major differences in the effects between these two can be explained by several factors.
Renovations in detached houses are funded solely by the household, which often relies on one or two household incomes. Therefore, this might be the reason why the detached housing market values both current state of the property in terms of energy efficiency and its potential energy efficiency higher than apartments, as all renovation costs and energy consumption bear a higher weight on the wallet than for those investing in apartments.
Moreover, detached houses are far more diverse in structure and size, whereas apartments are fairly homogeneous. In contrast to this, apartments, by their nature, often share walls and infrastructure, which limits the extent to which individual units can implement energy-saving technologies independently. Meanwhile, the flexibility of energy efficiency improvements is typically more apparent in detached houses.
Furthermore, energy costs and efficiency are aggregated at the building level for apartments. While any improvements in the building infrastructure can benefit all residents, individual unit owners may not directly perceive or control these benefits. This collective assessment can lead to a perception that personal investments in energy-efficient apartments, as indicated by its EPC label, may not yield a proportional financial return compared to detached houses. Leading to the effect of EPC labels being significantly less than the EPC label effect found for detached houses. Overall, the result appears to indicate that energy efficiency indicators and renovation potential toward energy efficiency differ across different property types. Nevertheless, these results must further be corroborated to ensure that the effects are actually significantly different from each other.

title: 6.3 Policy Effect
text:
Denmark introduced a policy on January 1, 2018, that imposed greater energy-efficiency restrictions for new buildings as well as tighter renovation standards for existing properties. The objective of this policy is to promote the development of energy-efficient properties and ensure that renovations made to existing properties improve overall energy performance. In this chapter, we explore whether the implementation of this policy has influenced home buyers’ perceptions of energy-efficient properties and their potential for energy efficiency.
Following the empirical strategy outlined by Jensen et al. (2016), we divide our sample according to the policy implementation date. Model 1 contains observations from before the policy was implemented, whereas Model 2 includes observations from after the policy was implemented. Both models represent Equation 7.2. The results are presented in Table 10.1.
Notably, before the implementation of the policy, label A2020 is found to have a negative but statistically insignificant effect, while labels A2010 and B are significant only at the 10% level. Additionally, label A2020, which was initially negative and statistically insignificant, gains a price premium of 6.2% compared to label D after the policy was implemented. Before the policy, the highest premium was found for properties labelled A2015, with a premium of 5.1% compared to label D. However, after the policy’s implementation, all energy-efficient labels, excluding A2015, experienced a significant increase in price premiums. The premium for label A2015 decreased, likely due to a stronger push towards higher-tier energy-efficient labels after the policy was enacted.
In addition to changes in the label effects, we also observe a significant change in home buyers’ perceptions of energy sources. While some energy sources experienced only marginal changes, others exhibited more substantial shifts. For instance, compared to district heating, properties heated solely with oil or with a combination of oil and electricity were sold at average discounts of 9.3% and 10.7%, respectively, before the policy. After the policy’s implementation, these discounts increased to 12.5% and 14.8%, respectively. At the same time, the price premiums associated with green energy systems, including heat pumps, solar cells, and solar heating, declined.
Overall, these results indicate that the implementation of the policy has not only shifted home buyers’ preferences towards more energy-efficient properties but also towards greater consideration of green energy sources, particularly district heating. However, this shift appears to have reduced the attention given to other green energy components, such as heat pumps, solar cells, and solar heating.
The policy also significantly affected the perceived energy-efficiency potential of properties. Following the policy’s implementation, home buyers placed greater value on the energy-efficiency potential of properties, resulting in higher price premiums for properties with greater potential to improve their EPC labels. While there were some changes in the types of renovations valued by consumers, these changes were relatively minor or negligible.
The results indicate that, following the implementation of the policy, home buyers’ preferences and market dynamics shifted in favour of energy efficiency. The policy coincided with a clear trend towards greater value being placed on energy-efficient properties, particularly those with higher EPC labels and greater potential for energy savings.

title: 6.4 Robustness Tests
text:
6.4 Robustness Tests
In this chapter, we assess the robustness of the main results and address potential limitations of the analysis. To do so, we conduct several alterations to the model specification and its variables. These modifications aim to evaluate the stability and reliability of our final specification, as detailed in Equation 7.2. The results are presented in Table 12.1 with Model 1 representing the main specification of Equation 7.2, corresponding to Model 6 in Table 8.1.

title: 6.4 Robustness Tests
text:
Outliers and Potential Data Errors
In Models 2 to 4, we alter the control and dependent variables by removing potential outliers and data errors to assess the robustness of our main results. In Model 2, we remove observations with sales prices greater than DKK 10 million (EUR 1.3 million). In Model 3, we exclude observations where the price per square metre is less than DKK [XX] (EUR 39) or greater than DKK 95,000 (EUR 12,350).
In Model 4, we remove observations based on selected control variables. Specifically, we exclude properties where the energy source is unknown, properties with more than four bathrooms or no bathroom, properties with more than four toilets, and properties with more than seven rooms or no rooms. In Model 5, we combine all the criteria from Models 2 to 4.
Across Models 2 to 5, the key variables do not appear to change substantially in terms of their signs or statistical significance. However, similar to the results found for the property-type segment, Model 5 shows that, on average, the most energy-efficient EPC label, A2020, does not appear to outperform label A2015 in terms of its price premium. This result provides further evidence of a potential non-linear relationship between energy efficiency and property prices. While energy-efficient properties are generally valued more highly than less energy-efficient properties, there appears to be a threshold beyond which additional improvements in energy efficiency do not translate into additional property value.
Regarding model fit, Model 5 produces a within \(R^2\) of up to 0.527, compared with 0.442 in our main specification (Model 6 in Table 8.1). This indicates that Model 5 explains 52.7% of the variation in property prices within the fixed-effects clusters.

title: 6.4 Robustness Tests
text:
Energy Consumption
Furthermore, we utilise the energy consumption of dwellings as an alternative measure of energy efficiency. In this specification, \(EE_i\) in Equation 7.2 represents the natural logarithm of the estimated annual energy consumption of dwelling \(i\), measured in kWh.
The purpose of using energy consumption is to assess whether the findings are consistent with those obtained using EPC labels. If a price premium is found for energy-efficient labels, where estimated energy consumption is an important determinant of these labels, one would expect energy consumption to produce similar results. Specifically, higher energy consumption should be associated with larger price discounts.
However, if this is not the case, one possible explanation is that the signalling effect of EPC labels is more important to consumers than the underlying estimated energy consumption. Consumers may not necessarily expect their actual energy consumption to correspond to the amount reported in the EPC report. This argument is consistent with the findings of Wahlström (2016).
For this interpretation to hold, however, we must assume that the EPC labels are genuinely capturing a signalling effect rather than incorporating other potential effects, such as omitted variables or measurement errors. Alternatively, differences between the effects of EPC labels and energy consumption could indicate potential bias or measurement error in our regression.
The results are presented in Model 6 and support the findings from the main analysis. Energy consumption has a negative and statistically significant effect on property prices at the 1% level. Based on the estimated coefficient, a 1% increase in energy consumption is associated with a 9.7% decrease in property prices. This result indicates that property prices are relatively elastic with respect to estimated energy consumption.
It is worth noting that, due to limitations in the data extraction process from the EPC reports, we were unable to extract estimated energy consumption for all properties. This is due both to data errors and to the fact that many EPC reports do not provide an estimate of energy consumption. Consequently, the sample used when analysing energy consumption contains 582,690 observations, which is approximately 20% smaller than the full sample used in the main analysis.

title: 6.4 Robustness Tests
text:
Robustness of Text Classification
Finally, we assess the robustness of the observed price premiums associated with solar heating, solar cells, and heat pumps, as reported in the main results (Model 6 in Table 8.1). We do this by estimating multiple models based on Equation 7.2 while continuously increasing the probability threshold used to classify the three variables.
The findings are presented in Table 12.2. As before, Model 1 represents the main specification, using an 85% probability threshold for all three variables. For Models 2 through 7, the probability thresholds are increased to 90%, 95%, 96%, 97%, 98%, and 99%, respectively.
For solar heating and solar cells, the coefficients are relatively stable, with only minor changes, and remain statistically significant at the 1% level across all specifications.
Interestingly, as the probability threshold for solar cells increases, the estimated price premium also increases, ranging from 3.35% to 4.48%. In contrast, the price premium associated with solar heating decreases as the probability threshold increases, ranging from 1.0% to 1.9%.
For heat pumps, the statistical significance changes from the 1% level in Model 1 to the 5% level for probability thresholds between 95% and 97%, before returning to the 1% level at the 98% and 99% thresholds. However, the estimated coefficient for heat pumps changes only marginally, ranging from 0.40% to 0.72%.
Moreover, the coefficients of the other key variables and control variables do not appear to change substantially as the probability threshold increases. It is worth noting that although increasing the probability threshold improves the precision of the classification by reducing the number of false-positive observations, this comes at the potential cost of increasing the number of false-negative observations.
Nevertheless, regardless of the probability threshold applied, all three components have a positive estimated effect on property prices. However, the relatively small and less stable coefficient for heat pumps suggests that home buyers may place less value on heat pumps compared with solar cells and solar heating.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
7. Conclusion and Discussion
This thesis set out to investigate whether home buyers are inattentive towards energy efficiency by utilising a unique and comprehensive dataset. The dataset was constructed from scratch by extracting and merging information from 776,106 EPC reports and more than 2.2 million property transactions. The main dataset consists of 728,794 residential property transactions in Denmark spanning from 1 July 2010 to 2023. Through the extraction and processing of information using regular expressions, OCR, and NLP techniques, and the subsequent merging with housing data, we have created a detailed dataset that allows for a multifaceted analysis of the relationship between energy efficiency and property prices. This enables us to account for a broader range of property characteristics, geographical factors, and information contained in EPC reports than is typically considered in the empirical analysis presented in the literature reviewed in this thesis.
The primary contribution of this study is threefold. First, unlike previous studies, which, to the best of our knowledge, have primarily focused on detached houses, this study broadens the analysis to include detached houses, row houses, duplexes, and apartments. This provides a more comprehensive perspective on how energy efficiency is valued across different segments of the housing market. Second, our study goes beyond EPC labels and estimated energy consumption by incorporating additional information from EPC reports concerning the potential for energy-efficient renovations. This allows us to investigate whether home buyers value not only the current energy efficiency of a property but also its potential for future improvements. Third, we examine whether the relationship between energy efficiency and property prices changed following the introduction of tighter energy-efficiency requirements in January 2018.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Main Findings
The results provide evidence that energy performance is an important factor in the valuation of residential properties in Denmark. Across the main specifications, properties with more energy-efficient EPC labels generally command higher prices than properties with label D, while properties with less energy-efficient labels generally sell at discounts. In Model 4, for example, properties labelled A2020, A2015, and A2010 command estimated premiums of 18.6%, 16.4%, and 11.3%, respectively, relative to label D. Properties labelled B and C command premiums of 7.6% and 4.7%, while properties labelled E, F, and G are associated with discounts of 7.9%, 15.8%, and 36.5%, respectively.
However, the estimated label effects become substantially smaller when additional information on renovation potential and more detailed time-by-geography fixed effects are introduced. In the final specification, the premiums associated with A2020, A2015, and A2010 decrease to 7.7%, 6.4%, and 2.6%, respectively, while the premiums for B and C are 2.2% and 2.0%. At the same time, the discounts associated with E, F, and G remain sizeable at 6.2%, 12.5%, and 28.7%, respectively.
This reduction in the EPC label effects is an important finding for the interpretation of the results. It suggests that part of the relationship between EPC labels and property prices may be related to characteristics that are correlated with energy efficiency and are not captured when considering the EPC label alone. In particular, the results indicate that renovation potential contains relevant information for property valuation. Consequently, estimates that focus only on EPC labels may overstate the extent to which the label itself captures the value placed on energy efficiency.
The findings therefore provide a more nuanced answer to the question of whether home buyers are inattentive towards energy efficiency. The results do not suggest that home buyers are generally inattentive to energy efficiency. Instead, they suggest that buyers respond to several dimensions of energy efficiency, but that these dimensions are not valued equally.

title: 7. Discussion
section: Energy Efficiency Beyond the EPC Label
text:
Energy Efficiency Beyond the EPC Label
An important finding of this thesis is that home buyers appear to value the potential for future improvements in energy efficiency. When renovation characteristics are incorporated into the final specification, the potential energy label resulting from implementing the renovation suggestions has a significant relationship with property prices. The relationship is also non-linear. A one-label improvement in potential energy efficiency has a relatively small positive effect, while greater potential initially increases the price effect before the relationship becomes negative for sufficiently large potential improvements.
This pattern suggests that renovation potential may contain two opposing signals for potential buyers. On the one hand, the possibility of improving a property’s energy efficiency may represent an opportunity to increase the property’s quality and reduce future energy consumption. On the other hand, a large improvement potential may also signal that the property currently requires substantial renovation. Thus, a high potential EPC improvement may simultaneously represent an opportunity and an indication of the investment required to realise that opportunity.
The results for the estimated costs and benefits of renovations provide further support for this interpretation. The estimated total energy cost saved and the estimated investment cost associated with profitable renovations have relatively modest and inelastic effects on property prices. This suggests that home buyers may not place the same weight on the generalised monetary estimates provided in the EPC reports as they do on more tangible characteristics of the property and its renovation potential.
This distinction is important when considering the question of inattention. The findings do not necessarily indicate that buyers ignore energy-related information. Instead, they may indicate that buyers place greater weight on information that is easier to relate to the physical condition and characteristics of the property than on generalised estimates of future monetary savings and renovation costs.
The results for specific renovation recommendations reinforce this interpretation. For example, properties for which an upgrade to district heating is suggested are associated with a 7.8% higher price, whereas properties with recommendations concerning windows or doors are associated with a 5.3% lower price. These results suggest that the type of renovation matters, rather than renovation potential being valued uniformly across all possible improvements.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Non-linear Effects of Energy Efficiency
The results also provide evidence of a potential non-linear relationship between energy efficiency and property prices. This pattern emerges both in the analysis across property types and in the robustness tests.
Across property types, detached houses generally exhibit the largest premiums for highly energy-efficient EPC labels. Compared with label D, detached houses with A2020, A2015, A2010, and B labels are associated with premiums of 15.2%, 16.6%, 9.9%, and 8.7%, respectively. The corresponding premiums are considerably smaller for apartments. For example, the estimated premiums for A2020, A2015, and B apartments are all approximately 3.7%, while the premium for A2010 is 5.4%.
The pattern across labels also suggests diminishing returns to increasingly high energy efficiency. In several specifications, the most energy-efficient label does not necessarily command a larger premium than the immediately preceding A label. This is particularly visible in the robustness tests, where A2020 does not consistently outperform A2015. Similarly, the property-type analysis indicates that premiums may decline once a property reaches the highest levels of energy efficiency.
One possible interpretation is that moving from a relatively inefficient property towards a high level of energy efficiency provides substantial perceived benefits, while further improvements beyond an already high level of efficiency provide increasingly smaller additional benefits. The results are therefore consistent with diminishing marginal valuation of energy efficiency. However, these findings should be interpreted as evidence of a potential non-linear relationship rather than as definitive evidence of a specific behavioural mechanism.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Differences Across Property Types
The analysis of different property types demonstrates that the value associated with energy efficiency is not uniform across the housing market. Detached houses generally display the strongest relationship between EPC labels and property prices, whereas the effects for apartments are considerably smaller. The results for duplexes are less precise, which is likely related to the substantially smaller sample of 8,236 observations. Consequently, the results for duplexes should be interpreted with greater caution.
The difference between detached houses and apartments may partly reflect the way energy-related investments and costs are distributed. For detached houses, renovation decisions, energy consumption, and associated costs are more directly connected to the individual household. In apartment buildings, by contrast, some energy-related characteristics and renovation costs are assessed at the building level and are therefore shared across multiple units.
This distinction is particularly relevant for the estimated energy costs and investment costs in the EPC reports. For detached houses, these estimates relate directly to the individual property, whereas for apartments they can relate to the entire apartment block. Consequently, the monetary benefits and costs associated with energy-efficiency improvements may be perceived differently by buyers of apartments and detached houses.
The property-type results therefore suggest that the same EPC information does not necessarily have the same economic meaning across different housing-market segments. Energy efficiency may be more directly observable and actionable for buyers of detached houses, while the collective nature of apartment buildings may weaken the relationship between individual EPC characteristics and property prices.
At the same time, these explanations should be treated as potential mechanisms rather than established causal explanations. The analysis identifies differences in estimated effects across property types, but further statistical testing would be required to establish whether the coefficients are statistically different from one another and to identify the mechanisms behind these differences.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Energy Sources and Systems
The results also show that home buyers respond to the energy source and heating systems of a property in addition to the EPC label itself. District heating is generally associated with relatively favourable prices, while properties relying on fossil fuels, particularly oil, tend to be associated with lower prices.
In the main specification, properties using natural gas, oil, or a combination of electricity and oil are associated with discounts relative to district heating, while some combinations involving electricity are associated with premiums. The property-type analysis further shows that the value associated with different energy sources varies substantially across housing segments.
The results for specific energy systems are also informative. Solar cells, solar heating, and heat pumps are generally associated with positive price effects in the main analysis, although the magnitude and statistical significance vary across property types and specifications. In particular, the effect of heat pumps is less stable than the effects of solar cells and solar heating.
The robustness analysis provides additional support for the positive association between these systems and property prices. Increasing the classification threshold for the NLP-based variables does not substantially alter the coefficients of the other key variables, while the coefficients for solar cells and solar heating remain positive and statistically significant. The heat-pump coefficient remains positive but exhibits greater variation in statistical significance.
Taken together, these results suggest that home buyers appear to respond to tangible energy-related characteristics of properties. However, the variation across energy sources and systems indicates that energy efficiency is not valued as a single homogeneous characteristic.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
The 2018 Policy Change
The analysis of the period before and after the implementation of the 2018 policy provides evidence of a change in the relationship between energy efficiency and property prices. Before the policy, A2020 was negative and statistically insignificant, while A2010 and B were significant only at the 10% level. Following the implementation of the policy, A2020 is associated with a 6.2% premium relative to label D, and the other energy-efficient labels, with the exception of A2015, experience increases in their estimated premiums.
The results also indicate a stronger preference for district heating following the policy implementation. Discounts associated with oil and the combination of oil and electricity increased from 9.3% to 12.5% and from 10.7% to 14.8%, respectively. At the same time, the estimated premiums associated with heat pumps, solar cells, and solar heating declined.
The analysis also suggests that the value associated with energy-efficiency potential increased after the policy was implemented, while changes in the types of renovations valued by consumers were relatively small.
Taken together, these results are consistent with a shift in the relationship between energy efficiency and property prices following the implementation of the policy. In particular, the results suggest greater valuation of higher EPC performance, energy-efficiency potential, and district heating.
However, these findings should not be interpreted as definitive evidence that the 2018 policy itself caused the observed changes. The post-policy period contains several other important changes that could potentially affect the housing market and the valuation of energy efficiency. In particular, the period following the policy implementation includes the COVID-19 pandemic and the energy price shock following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Therefore, the observed differences between the pre- and post-policy periods may reflect a combination of the policy and other changes occurring over the same period.
A more detailed identification strategy would therefore be required to isolate the causal effect of the policy from these other developments.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Robustness of the Findings
The robustness tests provide overall support for the main findings. Removing observations based on transaction prices, price per square metre, and selected property characteristics does not substantially change the signs or statistical significance of the key variables. This suggests that the main relationship between EPC characteristics and property prices is not driven solely by the particular observations removed in these specifications.
The use of estimated energy consumption as an alternative measure of energy efficiency provides further support for the main results. Energy consumption has a negative and statistically significant relationship with property prices, with a 1% increase in estimated energy consumption associated with a 9.7% decrease in property prices. This is consistent with the broader finding that lower energy consumption and greater energy efficiency are associated with higher property prices.
However, the energy-consumption analysis is based on a substantially smaller sample of 582,690 observations because estimated energy consumption could not be extracted for all properties. This limitation should therefore be considered when interpreting the result.
The time-on-the-market analysis also supports the main findings. Energy-efficient properties sell faster than D-labelled properties, while less energy-efficient properties take longer to sell. Interestingly, A2010 properties sell the fastest, followed by A2020 and A2015 properties. This ordering again provides evidence consistent with a non-linear relationship between energy efficiency and housing-market outcomes.
Taken together, the robustness tests suggest that the main findings are not solely dependent on the precise specification of the dependent variable, the treatment of potential outliers, or the classification thresholds used for the NLP-derived variables. Nevertheless, each robustness test has its own limitations, and the results should therefore be viewed as complementary evidence rather than as definitive proof of a single underlying mechanism.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Implications for the Research Question
The central question of this thesis is whether home buyers are inattentive towards energy efficiency. Based on the results, the answer appears to be more nuanced than a simple yes or no.
The results provide clear evidence that energy efficiency is reflected in property prices. Energy-efficient EPC labels are generally associated with higher prices, while inefficient labels are associated with lower prices. Home buyers also appear to value specific energy sources and systems, as well as the potential for future improvements in energy efficiency.
At the same time, the magnitude of the EPC label effect changes considerably once renovation potential and more detailed fixed effects are incorporated. Furthermore, the estimated monetary benefits from future energy savings and the investment costs of profitable renovations have relatively modest and inelastic effects. These findings suggest that home buyers do not necessarily treat all energy-related information in the EPC reports equally.
Thus, rather than characterising home buyers as simply inattentive, the results suggest that their valuation of energy efficiency may be selective. Buyers appear to place value on observable EPC labels, specific energy systems, and renovation potential, while the estimated monetary implications of future energy savings and renovation expenditures appear to receive less weight.
This distinction is important. If buyers were entirely inattentive to energy efficiency, we would not expect such consistent relationships between EPC labels, energy systems, renovation potential, and property prices. Conversely, the reduction in the EPC label effects after controlling for renovation potential indicates that the label alone should not be interpreted as a complete measure of how buyers value energy efficiency.
The findings therefore suggest that the information contained in EPC reports may affect property valuation through several different channels. The current energy performance of the property, the type of energy system, and the possibility of future improvements appear to matter, but their effects differ in magnitude and across property types. The results consequently point towards a more complex relationship between information, perceived property quality, renovation requirements, and energy efficiency than can be captured by EPC labels alone.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Limitations and Further Research
Despite the comprehensive nature of the dataset and our efforts to account for a wide range of property characteristics and geographical factors, we cannot rule out the possibility of omitted-variable bias. Factors such as the view from a property, local school quality, and crime rates may influence property prices but are not fully accounted for in the analysis. The inclusion of high-dimensional fixed effects helps account for some unobserved geographical and temporal heterogeneity, but it cannot eliminate all potential sources of omitted-variable bias.
Furthermore, the hedonic price framework does not allow us to fully disentangle supply- and demand-side effects. The estimated relationships therefore describe how energy-related characteristics are reflected in transaction prices, but they do not necessarily identify the separate contributions of buyers’ willingness to pay and sellers’ decisions to supply properties with particular characteristics.
The results also highlight several areas for further investigation. First, the non-linear relationship between EPC labels and property prices warrants further analysis. In particular, the finding that A2020 does not consistently command a higher premium than A2015 suggests that the marginal value of increasingly high energy efficiency may decline.
Second, the differences between detached houses and apartments deserve further investigation. The building-level nature of energy-cost and investment estimates for apartments may contribute to the smaller effects observed in this market segment. However, further analysis is needed to determine whether these differences are statistically significant and to identify the mechanisms underlying them.
Third, the robustness results indicate that the heat-pump coefficient is less stable than those of solar cells and solar heating. Further analysis distinguishing between different types of heat pumps could therefore provide a more detailed understanding of how these systems are valued.
Finally, the distribution of EPC labels in the sample raises an additional data-related concern. As shown in Figure ?fig-epc-population-vs-sample in ?sec-appendix-additional-figures, the sample contains relatively few observations for label A2015. The sample therefore does not appear to fully align with the population distribution of the three A labels. This discrepancy may affect the interpretation of comparisons between the A-label categories and warrants further investigation.

title: 7. Discussion
text:
Conclusion
Overall, this thesis provides evidence that energy efficiency is reflected in Danish residential property prices, but that its valuation is more complex than a simple relationship between EPC labels and transaction prices. Home buyers appear to value current energy performance, specific energy sources and systems, and the potential for future improvements. However, the substantially smaller EPC label effects after accounting for renovation potential indicate that part of the observed label premium may reflect other characteristics associated with energy efficiency.
The results further suggest that the relationship between energy efficiency and property prices may be non-linear, with diminishing returns at higher levels of energy efficiency. This pattern is observed across property types and is further supported by the robustness analysis using time on the market and alternative specifications.
The findings therefore do not support the conclusion that home buyers are simply inattentive towards energy efficiency. Instead, they suggest that buyers appear to pay attention to energy efficiency, but selectively. Tangible and readily observable characteristics of energy performance appear to matter more than generalised estimates of future energy savings and renovation costs. Moreover, the importance of these characteristics differs substantially across property types.
The 2018 policy analysis provides evidence of a change in the valuation of energy efficiency following the policy’s implementation, including greater premiums for several energy-efficient labels, greater valuation of energy-efficiency potential, and a stronger preference for district heating. However, given the other major developments occurring during the post-policy period, these results should be interpreted as changes associated with the post-policy period rather than as definitive causal effects of the policy.
Taken together, the results demonstrate the value of extracting information beyond the EPC label itself. The additional information contained in EPC reports provides important insights into how energy efficiency is incorporated into property prices and suggests that understanding the housing-market value of energy efficiency requires consideration of both the current state of a property and its potential future improvements. The unique dataset developed in this thesis provides a foundation for further research into these relationships and for more detailed investigation of how home buyers perceive and value energy-efficiency information.
